column1: Unit 1: What is real estate brokerage?
column2: The business of bringing buyers and sellers, landlords and tenants, or other parties together in real estate transactions.

column1: Unit 1: What does an appraiser do?
column2: An appraiser develops an opinion of property value, usually for lending, sale, tax, or legal purposes.

column1: Unit 1: What does a property manager do?
column2: A property manager operates real estate for an owner, including rent, maintenance, tenants, budgets, and reports.

column1: Unit 1: What does a mortgage lender do?
column2: A mortgage lender provides financing so buyers can purchase or refinance real estate.

column1: Unit 1: What does a real estate developer do?
column2: A developer improves land or existing property for a new or more profitable use.

column1: Unit 1: What is real estate counseling?
column2: Professional advice about real estate decisions, investments, use, value, or strategy.

column1: Unit 1: What is real estate investment?
column2: Buying, owning, or financing real estate to earn income, appreciation, tax benefits, or portfolio growth.

column1: Unit 1: What is supply in real estate?
column2: The amount of property available for sale or rent in a market.

column1: Unit 1: What is demand in real estate?
column2: The desire and ability of buyers or tenants to purchase or lease property.

column1: Unit 1: What happens when demand rises and supply is limited?
column2: Prices and rents usually rise because more people compete for fewer properties.

column1: Unit 1: Why is location so important?
column2: Location affects desirability, access, schools, jobs, amenities, safety perceptions, and value.

column1: Unit 1: Why are real estate markets local?
column2: Properties are fixed in place, and values depend on local supply, demand, economy, and neighborhood conditions.
The personal preference people have for one location over another.

column1: Unit 1: What is scarcity in real estate?
column2: Limited availability of land or desirable property in a specific market.
A human-made addition to land, such as a building, road, fence, or utility connection.

column1: Unit 1: What is permanence of investment?
column2: The long-term nature of improvements and capital invested in real estate.
People’s preference for certain neighborhoods or areas, also called situs.

column1: Unit 1: What is the role of a title company?
column2: To help research title, provide title insurance, and support closing or settlement.

column1: Unit 1: What is the role of an inspector?
column2: To evaluate property condition and report defects or safety concerns.

column1: Unit 1: What is the big exam idea from Unit 1?
column2: Real estate value is local and shaped by careers, services, supply, demand, and location.
The earth’s surface, subsurface, airspace, and things naturally attached to it.
Land plus permanent human-made improvements attached to the land.
Real estate plus the legal rights of ownership.
Movable property that is not permanently attached to land.
Another term for personal property.
Personal property that became real property because it was attached with intent to remain.

column1: Unit 2: What is a trade fixture?
column2: Business-related tenant property that may be removed if removal is timely and does not damage the property.
A right or item that belongs to and transfers with the land, such as an easement.

column1: Unit 2: What is the bundle of legal rights?
column2: The ownership rights to possess, control, enjoy, exclude, and dispose of property.

column1: Unit 2: What is the right of possession?
column2: The owner’s right to occupy or possess the property.

column1: Unit 2: What is the right of control?
column2: The owner’s right to use the property legally and within restrictions.

column1: Unit 2: What is the right of enjoyment?
column2: The owner’s right to use the property without unlawful interference.

column1: Unit 2: What is the right of exclusion?
column2: The owner’s right to keep others off the property, subject to law.

column1: Unit 2: What is the right of disposition?
column2: The owner’s right to sell, lease, will, or transfer the property.
The process of attaching personal property to real property.
The process of converting real property into personal property by detaching it.
Annual crops produced by tenant labor that are treated as personal property.

column1: Unit 2: What is the main fixture test?
column2: Attachment, adaptation, agreement, relationship of parties, and intent.
Rights to use or control space above land, within legal limits.
Rights to use or transfer interests below the earth’s surface, such as minerals.
The broadest ownership estate, potentially lasting forever.

column1: Unit 3: What is fee simple defeasible?
column2: Ownership that may end if a condition is violated.
Ownership lasting for the lifetime of a named person.
The person who holds property during the measuring life of a life estate.
A future interest that goes to a third party after a life estate ends.
A future interest returning to the original owner or heirs after a life estate ends.
A tenant’s right to possess property without owning it.
An ownership estate of uncertain duration.
A claim, charge, or liability affecting title or use.
A right to use another person’s land for a specific purpose.
An easement attached to and benefiting another parcel of land.

column1: Unit 3: What is easement in gross?
column2: An easement benefiting a person or company rather than a parcel.
An unauthorized physical intrusion onto another property.
A claim against property as security for a debt.
A private limit on property use written into a deed or covenant.
Government power to regulate for health, safety, morals, and welfare.
Government power to take private property for public use with compensation.
Government power to tax real property.
Transfer of property to the state when an owner dies without heirs.
The legal process used to exercise eminent domain.
Ownership by one person or one legal entity.
Ownership by two or more people or entities.

column1: Unit 4: What is tenancy in common?
column2: Co-ownership allowing unequal shares and inheritance by heirs.
Co-ownership usually requiring equal shares and right of survivorship.

column1: Unit 4: What is right of survivorship?
column2: A deceased owner’s interest passes to surviving co-owners.
Legal action to divide or sell co-owned property.

column1: Unit 4: What is tenancy by the entirety?
column2: Spousal ownership form with survivorship, recognized in some states.
Marital property system used in some states.
Property owned individually by one spouse.

Parts of a condo property owned or used by unit owners collectively.

column1: Unit 4: What is limited common elements?

Legal entity that may own real estate separately from shareholders.
Business association that may own real estate.
Limited liability company, a common entity for owning property.
Group pooling resources for a real estate investment.
A precise description identifying a specific parcel of land.

Measurements or distances in a metes-and-bounds description.
Boundaries or directions in a metes-and-bounds description.

column1: Unit 5: What is point of beginning?

Reference point or surface for elevations.

column1: Unit 6: What is legal description in a deed?

column1: Unit 6: What is delivery and acceptance?

column1: Unit 6: What is deed in trust?

column1: Unit 10: What is agency relationship in agreement?

column1: Unit 10: What is termination of listing?
column2: Ending the listing by expiration, agreement, breach, death, destruction, or law.

column1: Unit 10: What is ready willing and able buyer?
